source.name: OER Commons / CNCF open cloud-native curriculum

course.title: Kubernetes & Cloud-Native
course.description: Run containerized applications the way production teams do: declarative manifests, self-healing workloads, service networking, configuration, storage, scaling, safe rollouts, packaging with Helm, and observability. You will read real kubectl commands and YAML and practice applying them. Structure adapted from open cloud-native curricula on OER Commons (CC BY 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: A container image is best described as...
options: a running virtual machine with its own kernel
a packaged, immutable bundle of an app plus its dependencies
a physical server in a data center
questions.explanation: An image is a static, layered bundle; a container is a running instance of it. See 'From containers to clusters'.

questions.prompt: The smallest deployable unit you schedule in Kubernetes is...
questions.explanation: Kubernetes schedules Pods, which wrap one or more containers that share a network namespace. See 'Pods'.

questions.prompt: Which command applies a manifest file to a cluster?
questions.explanation: kubectl apply -f reconciles the cluster toward the desired state in the file. See 'Deployments and ReplicaSets'.

questions.prompt: Kubernetes is fundamentally a system for...
questions.explanation: You declare the desired state; controllers continuously drive the actual state toward it. See 'The Kubernetes architecture'.

questions.prompt: Which object gives a stable address to a changing set of Pods?
questions.explanation: A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of matching Pods. See 'Services and networking'.

questions.prompt: If a Pod crashes, what normally restarts it back to the desired count?
options: a human running kubectl by hand
its controller reconciling the desired replica count
questions.explanation: A controller such as a Deployment notices actual is below desired and creates a replacement. See 'Scaling and self-healing'.

questions.prompt: Sensitive values like passwords should be stored in...
options: a command-line flag in source control
questions.explanation: Secrets are the object meant for confidential data; ConfigMaps are for non-secret configuration. See 'ConfigMaps and Secrets'.

questions.prompt: What does a rolling update do?
options: gradually replaces old Pods with new ones to avoid downtime
rolls the cluster back to install time
questions.explanation: It swaps Pods incrementally, keeping the app available throughout. See 'Rolling updates and rollbacks'.

lessons.title: From containers to clusters: why orchestration
lessons.grammar_note: An image is the immutable package; a container is a running instance of that image. Keep the two words distinct.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a container is, name the problems that appear once you run many containers across many machines, and say in one sentence what an orchestrator gives you. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what is the difference between an image and a container?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A container packages an application together with its libraries and runtime so it runs the same way anywhere. Running one container on your laptop is easy. Running fifty across ten machines is not: something has to decide which machine each container lands on, restart the ones that die, replace machines that fail, give containers stable names so they can find each other, roll out new versions without downtime, and scale the count up and down with load. Doing that by hand does not survive contact with production. An orchestrator does it for you. Kubernetes is the orchestrator that won: you describe the desired state (how many copies, which image, how much memory), and it continuously works to make the real state match. A cluster is the pool of machines Kubernetes manages, plus the control plane that manages them.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
You can start a container directly with the runtime:
  docker run -d -p 8080:80 nginx:1.25
That runs exactly one copy on one host. If it crashes, it stays down. If the host dies, so does your app. Now compare the Kubernetes way: you do not run the container, you declare that you want three of them and let a controller keep three alive:
  kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.25 --replicas=3
  kubectl get pods
The second command lists the three running Pods. Kill one with 'kubectl delete pod <name>' and a replacement appears within seconds, because the declared desired count is three.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) True or false: a container carries its own operating system kernel. 2) Name two jobs an orchestrator handles that are painful to do by hand. 3) What is a cluster? 4) In the Kubernetes model, do you tell the system the exact steps to run, or the end state you want? 5) After 'kubectl create deployment web --replicas=3', how many Pods should be running? Answers: 1) False; containers share the host kernel and isolate at the process level. 2) Any two of: scheduling onto machines, restarting failed containers, replacing failed machines, service discovery, rolling updates, autoscaling. 3) The pool of machines Kubernetes manages together with its control plane. 4) The end state (desired state); Kubernetes figures out the steps. 5) Three.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating containers like tiny virtual machines with their own kernel; they share the host kernel. Mistake: assuming Kubernetes runs your containers once, like docker run; it maintains a desired count over time. Exit: (a) In one phrase, what problem does an orchestrator solve? (b) What word describes the state you declare versus the state Kubernetes observes? Answers: keeping many containers running correctly across many machines; the state you declare is the desired state (versus the actual state).

lessons.title: The Kubernetes architecture: control plane and nodes
lessons.grammar_note: The control plane decides; the nodes run the workloads. kubectl talks only to the API server, never directly to a node.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the main control-plane components and node components, and trace what happens when you run 'kubectl apply'. Warm-up: which single component do all your kubectl commands actually talk to?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A cluster has two kinds of machines. The control plane is the brain. It contains the API server (the front door: every request goes through it), etcd (a consistent key-value store holding the entire cluster state), the scheduler (decides which node an unscheduled Pod should run on), and the controller manager (runs the control loops that drive actual state toward desired state). Worker nodes run the actual workloads. Each node runs the kubelet (an agent that starts and watches the Pods assigned to it), a container runtime (which actually runs the containers), and kube-proxy (which programs the node's networking so Services work). The pattern everywhere is the reconciliation loop: a controller observes desired versus actual, and acts to close the gap. Nothing is a one-time command; everything is a loop that keeps running.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Trace 'kubectl apply -f web.yaml': kubectl sends the manifest to the API server, which validates it and writes the desired state into etcd. The Deployment controller sees a new Deployment wanting three Pods and creates three Pod objects. The scheduler sees three unscheduled Pods and assigns each to a node. On each chosen node, the kubelet sees a Pod assigned to it and tells the runtime to pull the image and start the container. You can watch the machinery:
  kubectl get nodes
  kubectl get pods -o wide          # shows which node each Pod landed on
  kubectl get componentstatuses    # health of control-plane pieces
  kubectl describe node <node-name> # capacity and the Pods it hosts

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which component is the single entry point for all cluster operations? 2) Where is cluster state persistently stored? 3) Which component picks the node for a new Pod? 4) Which agent runs on each worker node and starts its Pods? 5) Does kubectl talk to nodes directly? Answers: 1) The API server. 2) etcd. 3) The scheduler. 4) The kubelet. 5) No; kubectl talks to the API server, which coordinates the rest.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking kubectl connects straight to worker nodes; it only ever calls the API server. Mistake: expecting a controller to act once and stop; controllers loop forever, re-checking desired versus actual. Exit: (a) Name the four core control-plane components. (b) Name the three components on a worker node. Answers: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager; kubelet, container runtime, kube-proxy.

lessons.title: Pods: the unit of scheduling
lessons.grammar_note: You rarely create bare Pods in production. You create controllers (like Deployments) that create Pods for you, so failures are healed automatically.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define what a Pod is, write a minimal Pod manifest, and explain why containers in one Pod are tightly coupled. Warm-up: what is the smallest thing Kubernetes actually schedules?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A Pod is one or more containers that are always scheduled together on the same node and share a network namespace and storage volumes. Because they share the network namespace, containers in a Pod reach each other on localhost and share one IP address. Most Pods hold a single application container. A second container is added only when it directly supports the main one - a sidecar, for example one that ships logs. A Pod is mortal: it is never rescheduled to another node; if its node dies, the Pod is gone and a controller creates a new Pod with a new name and IP elsewhere. That is why you treat Pods as disposable and never hardcode a Pod IP.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
A minimal Pod manifest:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: hello
    labels:
      app: hello
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx:1.25
      ports:
      - containerPort: 80
Apply and inspect it:
  kubectl apply -f hello.yaml
  kubectl get pods
  kubectl describe pod hello        # events, image, node, restart count
  kubectl logs hello                # stdout of the container
  kubectl exec -it hello -- sh      # open a shell inside the container
Delete it and, because it is a bare Pod with no controller, nothing recreates it:
  kubectl delete pod hello

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How many IP addresses does a two-container Pod have? 2) How do containers in the same Pod talk to each other? 3) If a node dies, is its Pod moved to another node? 4) What field carries key-value tags used later by selectors? 5) Which command opens a shell inside a running Pod? Answers: 1) One; the containers share the Pod's network namespace. 2) Over localhost, since they share the network namespace. 3) No; the Pod is gone and a controller creates a fresh Pod elsewhere with a new name and IP. 4) metadata.labels. 5) kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: hardcoding a Pod's IP address; Pod IPs change every time a Pod is replaced. Mistake: stuffing unrelated apps into one Pod; put only tightly coupled containers together and scale independent apps as separate Pods. Exit: (a) What resources do containers in a Pod share? (b) Why do you usually let a controller create Pods instead of creating them directly? Answers: the same network namespace, IP, and storage volumes; so failed Pods are recreated automatically to maintain the desired count.

lessons.title: Deployments and ReplicaSets
lessons.grammar_note: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and a ReplicaSet manages Pods. You edit the Deployment; the layers below it are managed for you.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write a Deployment manifest, explain how selectors match Pods, and describe the Deployment-ReplicaSet-Pod hierarchy. Warm-up: what recreates a Pod after it is deleted?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A ReplicaSet has one job: keep exactly N copies of a Pod running, where N is spec.replicas. It uses a label selector to know which Pods it owns; if the count of matching Pods drops below N, it creates more. You almost never create a ReplicaSet directly. Instead you create a Deployment, which manages ReplicaSets for you and adds versioned rollouts: when you change the Pod template (say a new image), the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts Pods from the old one to the new one gradually. So the ownership chain is Deployment owns ReplicaSet owns Pods. The selector is the glue: the labels in spec.selector.matchLabels must match the labels in the Pod template, or the controller will not recognize its own Pods.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
A Deployment for three web replicas:
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: web
  spec:
    replicas: 3
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: web
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: web
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.25
          ports:
          - containerPort: 80
Apply and observe the hierarchy:
  kubectl apply -f web.yaml
  kubectl get deployments
  kubectl get replicasets           # one RS owned by the Deployment
  kubectl get pods -l app=web       # three Pods matching the selector
Delete a Pod and the ReplicaSet immediately recreates it:
  kubectl delete pod -l app=web --field-selector status.phase=Running | head -1
  kubectl get pods -l app=web       # still three

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which object directly guarantees N running Pods? 2) Which object do you normally create, and what does it add over a ReplicaSet? 3) What must match between spec.selector.matchLabels and the Pod template? 4) If replicas is 3 and you delete one Pod, how many end up running? 5) What is the full ownership chain from top to bottom? Answers: 1) The ReplicaSet. 2) A Deployment; it manages ReplicaSets and adds versioned rollouts and rollbacks. 3) The labels; the selector labels must equal the Pod template labels. 4) Three; the ReplicaSet recreates the missing one. 5) Deployment owns ReplicaSet owns Pods.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: label selector and Pod template labels not matching, so the controller ignores its own Pods. Mistake: creating ReplicaSets by hand, losing the rollout and rollback features a Deployment provides. Exit: (a) What keeps the replica count correct? (b) What does a Deployment create when you change the Pod template? Answers: the ReplicaSet; a new ReplicaSet, into which Pods are shifted gradually.

questions.prompt: The single front door that every cluster request passes through is the...
questions.explanation: All operations go through the API server, which then persists state to etcd.

questions.prompt: Cluster state is persistently stored in...
questions.explanation: etcd is the consistent key-value store holding the whole cluster state.

questions.prompt: Containers within a single Pod communicate with each other over...
questions.explanation: They share one network namespace, so they reach each other on localhost.

questions.prompt: The object whose only job is to keep N Pod copies running is the...
questions.explanation: A ReplicaSet maintains the desired replica count via its label selector.

questions.prompt: You change a Deployment's image. What does the Deployment create?
questions.explanation: It creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts Pods to it gradually.

questions.prompt: Which command shows which node each Pod is running on?
questions.explanation: The -o wide output adds the node (and Pod IP) columns.

lessons.title: Services and networking
lessons.grammar_note: Pods are ephemeral and their IPs change; a Service gives a stable name and IP in front of them. Never target a Pod IP directly.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why Services exist, name the common Service types, and reach one Pod set from another by DNS name. Warm-up: why can't you rely on a Pod's IP address?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Pods come and go, and each new Pod gets a new IP, so you cannot connect clients to Pod IPs. A Service is a stable abstraction: it gets a fixed virtual IP and a DNS name, and it uses a label selector to track the current set of healthy Pods, load-balancing traffic across them. The main types: ClusterIP (the default) is reachable only inside the cluster and is how one workload calls another; NodePort exposes the Service on a fixed port on every node; LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider for an external load balancer. Inside the cluster, a Service named 'web' in namespace 'default' is reachable at the DNS name web.default.svc.cluster.local, or just 'web' from the same namespace. That name is what you put in your app's config, not an IP.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
A ClusterIP Service in front of the Pods labeled app: web:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: web
  spec:
    selector:
      app: web
    ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
Apply and inspect it:
  kubectl apply -f web-svc.yaml
  kubectl get svc web               # shows the stable ClusterIP
  kubectl get endpoints web         # the Pod IPs currently behind it
From another Pod, reach it by name rather than IP:
  kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- http://web:80
Because the Service selector is app: web, endpoints update automatically as Pods are added or removed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why does a client target a Service instead of a Pod? 2) Which Service type is reachable only inside the cluster? 3) Which type requests an external load balancer from the cloud? 4) How does a Service know which Pods to send traffic to? 5) From the same namespace, what short name reaches a Service called 'web'? Answers: 1) Because Pod IPs change while a Service IP and DNS name stay stable. 2) ClusterIP. 3) LoadBalancer. 4) Through its label selector, which tracks matching healthy Pods. 5) Just 'web' (full form web.default.svc.cluster.local).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: connecting to a Pod IP, which breaks the moment the Pod is replaced. Mistake: a Service selector that does not match any Pod labels, giving an empty endpoints list and no traffic. Exit: (a) What two stable things does a Service provide? (b) What is the default Service type? Answers: a stable virtual IP and a DNS name; ClusterIP.

lessons.title: ConfigMaps and Secrets
lessons.grammar_note: ConfigMaps hold non-secret configuration; Secrets hold confidential data. Both decouple configuration from the image so you can reuse one image everywhere.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Externalize configuration from your image, choose between a ConfigMap and a Secret, and inject values as environment variables or files. Warm-up: why should a database password not be baked into a container image?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The same image should run in dev, staging, and production with only its configuration changing. ConfigMaps store non-secret key-value configuration (feature flags, URLs, tuning values). Secrets store confidential data (passwords, tokens, keys); their values are base64-encoded in the manifest and can be restricted more tightly by cluster policy. You consume either one two ways: as environment variables inside the container, or mounted as files in a volume. Mounting as files is handy for whole config files and for values you want to rotate without rebuilding the image. The point of both is decoupling: configuration lives in the cluster, not the image, so one immutable image serves every environment.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Create a ConfigMap and a Secret from the command line:
  kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info --from-literal=REGION=eu
  kubectl create secret generic db-cred --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret
Inject them into a Pod's container as environment variables:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: app
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: app
      image: myapp:1.0
      envFrom:
      - configMapRef:
          name: app-config
      env:
      - name: DB_PASSWORD
        valueFrom:
          secretKeyRef:
            name: db-cred
            key: DB_PASSWORD
Inspect them (note the value is stored base64-encoded):
  kubectl get configmap app-config -o yaml
  kubectl get secret db-cred -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Where should a public API URL go: ConfigMap or Secret? 2) Where should an access token go? 3) Name the two ways a container can consume a ConfigMap. 4) In what encoding are Secret values stored in the manifest? 5) What is the main reason to externalize configuration at all? Answers: 1) ConfigMap. 2) Secret. 3) As environment variables, or mounted as files from a volume. 4) base64. 5) So one immutable image can run unchanged across every environment, with only configuration differing.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming base64 is encryption; it is only encoding, so protect Secrets with access controls and do not commit them to source control. Mistake: putting confidential values in a ConfigMap. Exit: (a) Which object is for non-secret config? (b) Name one way to inject configuration into a container. Answers: a ConfigMap; environment variables or a mounted file.

lessons.title: Storage and volumes
lessons.grammar_note: A container's own filesystem is erased when the Pod is replaced. For data that must survive, use a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by a PersistentVolume.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain why container filesystems are ephemeral, and use a PersistentVolumeClaim to keep data across Pod restarts. Warm-up: what happens to files written inside a container when its Pod is deleted?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: By default, anything a container writes to its own filesystem disappears when the container is replaced - fine for a stateless web server, fatal for a database. Kubernetes separates the request for storage from the actual storage. A PersistentVolume (PV) is a piece of real storage in the cluster (a cloud disk, an NFS share). A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request for storage of a certain size and access mode; Kubernetes binds the claim to a matching PV, often provisioning it automatically through a StorageClass. Your Pod references the PVC and mounts it at a path. Because the PVC and its data live independently of any single Pod, a replacement Pod can mount the same claim and see the same data. Access modes matter: ReadWriteOnce means one node at a time, ReadWriteMany means many nodes at once.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Request 1Gi of persistent storage with a claim:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
  metadata:
    name: data
  spec:
    accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
    resources:
      requests:
        storage: 1Gi
Mount that claim into a Pod:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  metadata:
    name: db
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: db
      image: postgres:16
      volumeMounts:
      - name: data
        mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
    volumes:
    - name: data
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: data
Check the binding:
  kubectl get pvc data              # STATUS should read Bound
  kubectl get pv                    # the volume the claim bound to

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What happens to a container's local filesystem when the Pod is replaced? 2) What does a PersistentVolumeClaim represent? 3) What often provisions a PersistentVolume automatically? 4) What does ReadWriteOnce mean? 5) After a Pod using a PVC is deleted and recreated, is the data still there? Answers: 1) It is erased. 2) A request for storage of a given size and access mode. 3) A StorageClass. 4) The volume can be mounted read-write by a single node at a time. 5) Yes; the data lives with the PVC and its PV, not with the Pod.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: storing important data on the container filesystem and losing it on the next restart. Mistake: requesting ReadWriteMany from storage that only supports ReadWriteOnce, so the claim never binds. Exit: (a) Which object requests storage? (b) Which object is the real storage it binds to? Answers: a PersistentVolumeClaim; a PersistentVolume.

lessons.title: Scaling and self-healing
lessons.grammar_note: Self-healing depends on probes. A liveness probe restarts a stuck container; a readiness probe keeps traffic away from a Pod that is not ready.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Scale a Deployment manually and automatically, and use liveness and readiness probes so the cluster heals and routes correctly. Warm-up: what restarts a crashed Pod back to the desired count?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Scaling is just changing the desired replica count; the controller creates or removes Pods to match. You can set it by hand, or let a HorizontalPodAutoscaler adjust it based on a metric such as CPU. Self-healing has two halves. First, controllers keep the replica count correct: kill a Pod and a replacement appears. Second, probes tell Kubernetes about container health. A liveness probe checks whether the container is still working; if it fails repeatedly, the kubelet restarts that container. A readiness probe checks whether the container is ready to serve; while it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints so no traffic is sent to it, but it is not restarted. Together, these keep a service both available and correct under load and failure. Setting resource requests also lets the scheduler place Pods sensibly.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Scale by hand, then set up autoscaling:
  kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
  kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=3 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70
  kubectl get hpa
Add probes and resource requests to the container spec:
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx:1.25
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 100m
          memory: 128Mi
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 80
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /ready
          port: 80
        periodSeconds: 5
Watch a deleted Pod come back:
  kubectl delete pod -l app=web --grace-period=0 --force | head -1
  kubectl get pods -l app=web -w

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How do you manually scale a Deployment to 5 replicas? 2) What object scales replicas automatically based on a metric? 3) What does a failing liveness probe cause? 4) What does a failing readiness probe cause? 5) If you delete a Pod from a Deployment with replicas=3, what happens? Answers: 1) kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=5. 2) A HorizontalPodAutoscaler. 3) The kubelet restarts the container. 4) The Pod is pulled out of Service endpoints so it receives no traffic, without being restarted. 5) The ReplicaSet creates a replacement to restore the count to 3.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing liveness and readiness; liveness restarts a broken container, readiness only gates traffic. Mistake: expecting a HorizontalPodAutoscaler to work with no CPU or memory requests set, since it needs a baseline to compute percentages. Exit: (a) What is scaling, in terms of desired state? (b) Which probe controls whether a Pod receives traffic? Answers: changing the desired replica count so the controller adjusts the Pods; the readiness probe.

questions.prompt: A client should connect to a workload through a Service because...
options: the Service IP and DNS name stay stable while Pods change
questions.explanation: Pods are ephemeral; the Service abstraction stays put and tracks healthy Pods.

questions.prompt: Confidential values such as passwords belong in a...
questions.explanation: Secrets are the object for confidential data; ConfigMaps are for non-secret config.

questions.prompt: To keep data across Pod restarts you mount a...
questions.explanation: A PVC binds to a PersistentVolume whose data outlives any single Pod.

questions.prompt: A repeatedly failing liveness probe causes the kubelet to...
options: remove the Pod from Service endpoints only
questions.explanation: Liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure only gates traffic.

questions.prompt: Which object automatically adjusts replica count from a metric like CPU?
questions.explanation: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales the Deployment between min and max.

questions.prompt: Base64 encoding of a Secret value provides...
questions.explanation: base64 is encoding; protect Secrets with access controls, not by assuming secrecy.

lessons.title: Rolling updates and rollbacks
lessons.grammar_note: maxUnavailable and maxSurge control how aggressively a rollout swaps Pods. Conservative values keep the app available throughout.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Roll out a new version without downtime, watch the rollout, and roll back to the previous version when something breaks. Warm-up: what object does a Deployment create when the Pod template changes?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: When you change a Deployment's Pod template - typically the image tag - the Deployment performs a rolling update: it creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually shifts Pods from the old one to the new one, so some replicas are always serving. Two settings tune the pace. maxUnavailable is how many replicas may be down at once during the rollout; maxSurge is how many extra replicas may be created above the desired count. The Deployment keeps a history of previous ReplicaSets, so if the new version misbehaves you can roll back to the prior revision quickly. The whole thing is still declarative: you state the new desired template, and the controller reconciles toward it Pod by Pod. Health probes matter here too, since the rollout waits for new Pods to become ready before continuing.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Trigger and watch a rolling update, then roll it back:
  kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.27
  kubectl rollout status deployment/web       # progress until complete
  kubectl get rs -l app=web                    # old RS scaling down, new scaling up
  kubectl rollout history deployment/web       # list of revisions
  kubectl rollout undo deployment/web          # back to the previous revision
  kubectl rollout undo deployment/web --to-revision=2
Tune the strategy in the Deployment spec:
  spec:
    strategy:
      type: RollingUpdate
      rollingUpdate:
        maxUnavailable: 1
        maxSurge: 1
Pause and resume a rollout to batch several edits:
  kubectl rollout pause deployment/web
  kubectl rollout resume deployment/web

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What kind of update does changing the image trigger by default? 2) What does maxSurge control? 3) What does maxUnavailable control? 4) Which command returns the app to its previous version? 5) Why can Kubernetes roll back at all? Answers: 1) A rolling update. 2) How many extra Pods above the desired count may be created during the rollout. 3) How many replicas may be unavailable at once during the rollout. 4) kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>. 5) Because the Deployment retains a history of previous ReplicaSets (revisions).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: setting maxUnavailable too high, so too many Pods drop at once and the service degrades mid-rollout. Mistake: rolling out an image with no readiness probe, so traffic hits Pods before they are ready. Exit: (a) What object holds the rollout history you roll back to? (b) Name the two settings that pace a rolling update. Answers: previous ReplicaSets (revisions) kept by the Deployment; maxUnavailable and maxSurge.

lessons.title: Helm and packaging
lessons.grammar_note: A chart is a template plus default values; a release is one installed instance of a chart with your values applied. Same chart, different values, different releases.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what problem Helm solves, describe a chart's structure, and install and upgrade a release with custom values. Warm-up: if you deploy the same app to dev and prod, what usually differs between them?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A real application is many manifests - Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, PVC - and you deploy near-identical copies to several environments that differ only in a few values. Copy-pasting YAML does not scale. Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a bundle of templated manifests plus a values.yaml holding defaults; you override values per environment. Installing a chart creates a release, a named, versioned instance tracked by Helm. Upgrading a release re-renders the templates with new values or a new chart version and applies the diff; if it goes wrong, Helm can roll the release back to a previous revision, much like a Deployment rollback but for the whole bundle. Charts can also depend on other charts, so you compose larger systems from reusable pieces.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
A chart directory looks like this:
  mychart/
    Chart.yaml        # name and version metadata
    values.yaml       # default values
    templates/
      deployment.yaml # uses {{ .Values.image.tag }} etc.
      service.yaml
Install, override values, upgrade, and roll back a release:
  helm install web ./mychart
  helm install web ./mychart --set image.tag=1.27
  helm install web ./mychart -f prod-values.yaml
  helm upgrade web ./mychart --set replicaCount=5
  helm list                          # releases and their revisions
  helm rollback web 1                # back to revision 1
  helm uninstall web
A template line reads a value like this:
  image: "nginx:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What problem does Helm solve? 2) What is a chart? 3) What is a release? 4) How do you override the default values for one environment? 5) Which command reverts a release to an earlier revision? Answers: 1) Managing and reusing many related manifests across environments without copy-pasting YAML. 2) A bundle of templated manifests plus default values. 3) A named, versioned installed instance of a chart. 4) With --set key=value or -f a custom values file. 5) helm rollback <release> <revision>.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: editing rendered manifests in the cluster by hand instead of the chart values, so the next helm upgrade overwrites your change. Mistake: confusing a chart (the package) with a release (one installed instance). Exit: (a) What file holds a chart's default values? (b) What command upgrades a release with new values? Answers: values.yaml; helm upgrade.

lessons.title: Observability: logs, metrics, and events
lessons.grammar_note: Logs tell you what one Pod did; metrics tell you how the whole system behaves over time; events tell you what Kubernetes itself decided.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a Pod's logs, inspect cluster events, check resource usage, and know when to reach for metrics versus logs. Warm-up: your Pod keeps restarting - which command shows why?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Observability is how you understand a running system. Three signals cover most needs. Logs are the text a container writes to stdout and stderr; you read them per Pod. Metrics are numeric time series - CPU, memory, request rate, error rate - collected by a metrics stack and graphed to show trends and trigger alerts. Events are records the cluster emits about its own decisions - scheduling, pulling images, failing probes, restarting containers - and they are the first place to look when a Pod will not start. A container that crashes on startup shows a CrashLoopBackOff status; its previous logs and its events usually reveal the cause. Good observability means you can answer what is broken, since when, and why, without guessing.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Read logs, including from a crashed previous container:
  kubectl logs web-5c8-abcde
  kubectl logs web-5c8-abcde --previous     # logs from the last crash
  kubectl logs -l app=web --tail=50 -f       # follow logs across matching Pods
Inspect events and status when a Pod misbehaves:
  kubectl get pods                            # look for CrashLoopBackOff or Pending
  kubectl describe pod web-5c8-abcde          # Events section at the bottom
  kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
Check live resource usage (requires the metrics stack):
  kubectl top pods
  kubectl top nodes

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which signal is the text a container writes to stdout? 2) Which signal is best for trends and alerting over time? 3) Where do you look first when a Pod will not start? 4) What status indicates a container repeatedly crashing on startup? 5) Which flag shows logs from the container instance before the latest restart? Answers: 1) Logs. 2) Metrics. 3) The Pod's events (kubectl describe pod, or kubectl get events). 4) CrashLoopBackOff. 5) --previous.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading only current logs for a CrashLoopBackOff, when the useful output is in the previous container's logs (--previous). Mistake: expecting kubectl top to work without a metrics stack installed. Exit: (a) Name the three core observability signals. (b) Which command lists cluster events newest last? Answers: logs, metrics, and events; kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp.

questions.prompt: The core operating model of Kubernetes is best summarized as...
options: declare desired state; controllers reconcile actual toward it
questions.explanation: You declare desired state and controllers loop to make actual state match.

questions.prompt: The ownership chain from top to bottom is...
questions.explanation: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which manage Pods.

questions.prompt: To expose a set of Pods at a stable in-cluster address you create a...
questions.explanation: A ClusterIP Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name inside the cluster.

questions.prompt: Non-secret configuration values belong in a...
questions.explanation: ConfigMaps hold non-secret config; Secrets hold confidential data.

questions.prompt: Data that must survive Pod replacement is kept with a...
questions.explanation: A PVC binds to a PersistentVolume whose data outlives any single Pod.

questions.prompt: During a rolling update, maxUnavailable controls...
options: extra Pods created above desired count
how many replicas may be down at once
the number of nodes in the cluster
questions.explanation: maxUnavailable caps downtime; maxSurge caps extra Pods above desired.

questions.prompt: To return a Deployment to its previous version you run...
questions.explanation: rollout undo reverts to the prior revision kept as a previous ReplicaSet.

questions.prompt: In Helm terms, one installed, versioned instance of a chart is called a...
questions.explanation: A chart is the package; a release is one installed instance of it.

questions.prompt: A Pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff is best diagnosed by...
options: kubectl logs --previous and kubectl describe pod
questions.explanation: Previous logs plus the Pod's events usually reveal why it crashes on startup.

questions.prompt: A readiness probe that is failing causes the Pod to...
options: be removed from Service endpoints until it passes
questions.explanation: Readiness gates traffic only; liveness is what restarts a container.

lessons.title: Capstone: deploy a small app to a cluster
lessons.grammar_note: Work declaratively: put every object in YAML, apply it, and verify with kubectl get and kubectl describe. If something is wrong, read the events before changing anything.

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Deploy a small stateless web application to a cluster and expose it, using only declarative manifests. You will create a Deployment with three replicas, a ClusterIP Service in front of it, a ConfigMap for its configuration, readiness and liveness probes, then perform a rolling update to a new image and a rollback. Assemble the manifests below, apply them, and verify each step with kubectl. Treat it as work you would hand to a teammate to review.

sections.heading: The manifests to assemble
sections.text:
Put these in one file, app.yaml, separated by --- document markers.
ConfigMap:
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ConfigMap
  metadata:
    name: web-config
  data:
    GREETING: hello-from-kubernetes
Deployment (three replicas, probes, config injected):
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: web
  spec:
    replicas: 3
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: web
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: web
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.25
          ports:
          - containerPort: 80
          envFrom:
          - configMapRef:
              name: web-config
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 80
Service (stable in-cluster address):
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Service
  metadata:
    name: web
  spec:
    selector:
      app: web
    ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80

sections.heading: The commands to run in order
sections.text: 1) Apply everything: kubectl apply -f app.yaml. 2) Confirm three Pods are Running and Ready: kubectl get pods -l app=web. 3) Confirm the Service has three endpoints: kubectl get endpoints web. 4) Reach the app from inside the cluster: kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- http://web:80. 5) Prove self-healing: kubectl delete pod -l app=web | head -1, then kubectl get pods -l app=web and watch a replacement appear so the count returns to three. 6) Roll out a new version: kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.27, then kubectl rollout status deployment/web. 7) Roll it back: kubectl rollout undo deployment/web, then kubectl rollout history deployment/web.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: all three Pods reach Running and Ready; kubectl get endpoints web lists three Pod IPs; the wget from a temporary Pod returns the nginx page over the Service name, not a Pod IP; after you delete a Pod the count returns to three on its own; kubectl rollout status reports the update completed successfully; kubectl rollout undo returns the Deployment to the prior revision and the app stays reachable throughout. If all six are true, you have deployed, exposed, healed, updated, and rolled back a workload the way a production team does.
